claim: Apel, Liebig, Brandl, Lengauer and Kastner 2011 (semistructured merge): on 180 Java merge scenarios, conflicts fell in 60 % of scenarios by 34 ± 21 % against unstructured line merge, and conflicting lines fell in 82 % of scenarios by 61 ± 22 % (real merge scenarios, no contention level controlled).
Apel et al. 2011 (semistructured merge): in 26 % (46 of 180) of Java merge scenarios, semistructured merge increased the number of conflicts, by 109 ± 170 %.
Apel et al. 2011: on 180 Java merge scenarios, line merge combined with semistructured merge had a further 35 % fewer conflicts than pure line merge.

Apel, Lessenich and Lengauer 2012 (JDime): structured merge with auto-tuning was up to 12 times faster than purely structured merge (5 times on average), on 72 merge scenarios from 8 Java projects of over 17 million lines of code.
Apel, Lessenich and Lengauer 2012 (JDime): structured merge with auto-tuning reports 39 % of the conflicts and 24 % of the conflicting lines of unstructured line merge, mostly ordering conflicts.
Apel, Lessenich and Lengauer 2012 (JDime): unstructured merge was up to 71 times faster than structured merge (15 times on average).
Apel, Lessenich and Lengauer 2012 (JDime): 21 % of changed files cannot be merged with unstructured merge; with structured merge this fraction falls to 15 %.
Cavalcanti, Borba and Accioly 2017 (OOPSLA): on 34,030 scenarios from 50 Java projects, semistructured merge left 14,544 conflicts against 19,238 for line merge, a reduction of about 24 %.

Cavalcanti, Borba and Accioly 2017 (OOPSLA): semistructured merge gave no evidence of fewer false negatives (clean merges that are wrong); additional false negatives were 20.60 ± 21.30 % for semistructured against 9.62 ± 16.29 % for line merge, stated as an overestimated upper bound.

Cavalcanti, Borba, Seibt and Apel 2019: on 43,509 scenarios from 508 Java projects, semistructured and structured merge differ in 24 % of scenarios with conflicts but in only 0.58 % (253) of all scenarios; false negatives were 39 for structured against 5 for semistructured.

Larsen, Falleri, Baudry and Monperrus 2022 (Spork, Java): on 1,740 real file merges from 119 open-source projects, Spork's conflicts were better than JDime and on par with AutoMergePTM; median merge time 1.17 s against 1.32 s (JDime) and 1.48 s (AutoMergePTM); no figure against line merge is given.
Larsen et al. 2022 (Spork): the tool ignores delete-versus-edit conflicts, so one side's deletion of a subtree silently overrides edits to it without a conflict.

Ellis, Nadi and Dig 2022 (RefMerge): on 2,001 merge scenarios from 20 projects, each chosen for a git refactoring-related conflict, RefMerge resolved or reduced conflicts in 497 (25 %) and increased conflicting lines in 214 (11 %); IntelliMerge resolved or reduced conflicts in 478 (24 %) and increased conflicting lines in 597 (30 %).
Ellis, Nadi and Dig 2022: on a hand-checked sample of 50 merge scenarios, git had 243 false positives and 5 false negatives, IntelliMerge 707 and 71, RefMerge 188 and 0.
handles: false positives false negatives merge tools

claim: Ellis, Nadi and Dig 2022: with a 15-minute timeout, RefMerge timed out on 382 merge scenarios and IntelliMerge on 870 in that study.

Khanna, Kunal and Pierce 2007 (diff3): diff3 is clean only when the edited regions satisfy stated conditions; with several edited regions the guarantee fails, and diff3 is neither idempotent nor stable.

Sousa, Dillig and Lahiri 2018 (SafeMerge): on 52 real GitHub merge scenarios, filtered to remove trivially conflict-free ones, SafeMerge verified 39 and warned on 13; eleven of the 13 were real semantic conflicts and two were false positives (false positive rate around 15 %); about 0.5 s to verify each benchmark.

Sousa, Dillig and Lahiri 2018 (SafeMerge): in the paper's comparison with kdiff3, 33 benchmarks were clean and verified, and kdiff3 gave five textual merges that were semantically incorrect, of which 3 were true (two were the false positives).

Sousa, Dillig and Lahiri 2018 (SafeMerge): the paper states that SafeMerge can automatically verify 75 % of the merge scenarios that occur in the wild; this is the paper's own statement, not a measurement in the collect file.

Da Silva, Borba and others 2023 (SAM, arXiv 2310.02395): generated unit tests detected nine of 28 known semantic conflicts in the best configuration, on 51 merge scenarios, with 5 minutes of test generation per tool.

Xu, Subramanian and Karthik 2026 (preprint, arXiv 2607.04697): a three-way git merge of AI-agent pull requests conflicted in 19.8 % (119 of 601; 95 % CI 16.8 to 23.2 %) of same-agent time-overlapping pairs and 41.7 % (48 of 115; CI 33.1 to 50.9 %) of cross-agent pairs.
handles: AI agent pull requests merge conflict rate

claim: Xu, Subramanian and Karthik 2026 (preprint): cross-agent pairs are only 0.50 % of 580,913 co-active pairs (2,896 pairs, in 122 of 2,807 repos), and about 42 % of conflicts are modify/delete or add/add.

Ogenrwot and Businge 2026 (AgenticFlict, AIware, arXiv 2604.03551): of 107,026 simulated merges of agent pull requests from 142,652 PRs in 59,412 repos, 29,609 conflicted, a 27.67 % conflict rate against the target branch (textual only; a PR-against-base rate, not a pair rate).
Ogenrwot and Businge 2026 (AgenticFlict): the textual conflict rate against base ran by agent from 15.24 % to 31.85 % in the table (the text gives 15.43 % for Copilot and 20.06 % for Cursor).

Ogenrwot and Businge 2026 (AgenticFlict): the conflict rate rises with PR size, about 9.9 % at a median churn of 2 lines, nearly 30 % at 25 lines and 32 to 33 % at 46 to 185 lines (PR-level, confounded).

Pugachev 2025 (CodeCRDT, one author, preprint): over 600 trials (6 TypeScript/React tasks, 50 runs per mode, Claude Sonnet 4.5, up to 5 parallel agents), parallel mode was 13.1 % slower overall, ranging from 21.1 % faster (Tic-Tac-Toe) to 39.4 % slower (Algorithm Visualizer).

Pugachev 2025 (CodeCRDT): a preliminary manual inspection of 60 of 600 runs suggested 5 to 10 % semantic conflicts (20 % for simple tasks, 80 % for complex tasks); parallel code volume was 82 to 189 % larger for complex tasks.
handles: semantic conflicts parallel agents manual inspection

claim: Yang, Nie and others 2026 (Co-Coder, preprint; greenfield generation, not edits to an existing repository; base model gpt-5-mini): on DevEval (10 Python projects), pass rate 56.8 % to 68.1 %, 1.81x speed-up and 28 % lower cost.
Yang, Nie and others 2026 (Co-Coder): on DevEval, file-per-agent parallel generation reached a 57.7 % pass rate and was 44 % dearer, so it was no better than the proposed method.

Yang, Nie and others 2026 (Co-Coder): on CodeProjectEval (18 projects, 11.9 files and 2,371 lines on average), pass rate 34.1 against 20.1 for sequential (points), latency 1315 s against 2756 s, cost $0.67 against $1.03.
Yang, Nie and others 2026 (Co-Coder): on CodeProjectEval, Claude Code with Agent Teams had the lowest latency (680 s) and cost ($0.38) but a 16.3 pass rate, below even the sequential baseline.
Yang, Nie and others 2026 (Co-Coder): edge density of the dependency graph correlates with gain (Pearson 0.65, 16 projects).

Liu, Chen, Xu, Jiang and Dong 2026 (STORM, preprint): one shared workspace with version-checked writes, with Sonnet 4.6 on Commit0-Lite and 4 engineers, reached an 82.5 % macro pass rate against 63.8 % for isolated git worktrees (+18.7 points).
handles: worktree versus shared workspace pass rate

claim: Liu et al. 2026 (STORM): across runs with 2, 4 and 8 engineers the overall pass rate ran from 38.2 % to 69.7 % while cost rose from $199 to $429, and wall-clock stayed roughly constant (13 hours total).

Liu et al. 2026 (STORM): even with a manager assigning disjoint file sets, 21.7 % of first-round tasks overlapped another's file scope at 4 engineers and 35.1 % at 8; first-round overlap correlated with rejected reviews (r = 0.78 within k = 8).
handles: manager disjoint file sets rejected reviews

claim: Liu et al. 2026 (STORM), the paper's own stated limits: file-level granularity makes two agents editing different functions in one file trigger a false-positive rejection, and bash writes bypass the check.

Geng and Neubig 2026 (CAID, preprint): a manager with up to N engineers in git worktrees reported +26.7 points absolute on PaperBench and +14.3 on Python library development tasks in the abstract (the figure shows +26.6 and +14.7) against a single agent.

Geng and Neubig 2026 (CAID): on Commit0-Lite with Claude 4.5, the single agent scored 53.1 % in 692.6 s for $1.9 and CAID 59.1 % in 1583.2 s for $8.1, about 2.3 times the wall-clock and 4.3 times the cost.

Geng and Neubig 2026 (CAID): isolated worktrees beat a shared workspace on Commit0-Lite (59.1 against 56.1) and PaperBench (63.3 against 55.5); on PaperBench the shared workspace's 55.5 was below the single agent's 57.2.
Geng and Neubig 2026 (CAID): performance improved from 2 to 4 engineers and decreased at 8 engineers (the paper's statement).

Shen, Zhang, Zhao, Liang and others 2019 (IntelliMerge, OOPSLA; read as an abstract only, body not read): on 1,070 merge scenarios from 10 Java projects, conflicts fell by 58.90 % against GitMerge on the authors' own scenario set, with auto-merging precision 88.48 % and recall 90.22 %.
